newsitem.title: UK: Flights, holidays not seen hit by fuel price jump.
newsitem.headline: Flights, holidays not seen hit by fuel price jump.

text.p: Flights and holidays will not be hit by the leap in jet fuel prices after U.S. missile strikes on Iraq, airlines and travel operators said on Thursday.
Airlines said sophisticated trading techniques had helped them avoid the sort of damage that some sustained when oil prices rocketed after the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
"We have a risk management plan in place which is designed to cope with this kind of eventuality," said a spokeswoman for British Airways, one of the world's largest carriers.

But oil traders were more sceptical, saying airlines had been hit by fuel costs that had risen sharply even before the recent action against Iraq -- a rise compounded by gains in the dollar, the currency of the international oil market.
This year's price for jet fuel is on average about 25 percent above 1995 levels.

"We estimate our jet costs will rise 20 to 30 percent this year compared to last," an oil trader for a European airline said. But he added that he expected only a modest amount of costs to be passed on to the consumer.
"Competition is severe so airlines don't want to raise prices in case they lose market share. But I do think (company) results will be hit," he said.
Holiday firms are also trying to keep their customers protected and see little chance of price hikes.

"A 10 percent rise in jet fuel prices usually means a one cent rise in costs to the tour operator," said Keith Betton, head of corporate affairs at the Association of British Travel Agent (ABTA), representing 620 tour operators and 7,000 travel agents.
For a short-haul holiday costing 300 pounds ($470), about 100 pounds goes to the airline. Of that, about 30 is for fuel.
A five percent price rise means just 1.50 pounds more -- well below the amount for which most travel companies would charge.
"Administration costs are more than the price hike itself so most won't bother," one industry source said.

The gains "will not have an impact on Thomson customers because we give a surcharge guarantee," said Ray Smith, financial controller of Thomson Tour Operations, Britain's largest operator. Jet fuel prices jumped about five percent this week to near $245 a tonne after an oil-for-food deal between Iraq and the United Nations was put on ice after Iraqi incursions in Kurdish areas. This mirrored a $1 a barrel leap for crude oil.
The price of jet reached around $500 a tonne after Iraq invaded Kuwait six years ago.
Oil traders think some airlines got it wrong this year by failing to buy during the summer when, for a few weeks, prices languished below $200 a tonne.

"They didn't want to buy in the spring because prices were too high and then they held off again, hoping the oil-for-food deal with Iraq would push prices lower," said a trader at a Wall Street bank who specialises in jet fuel.

Compounding the problem, European airlines are exposed to exchange rate movements as well as oil when buying fuel. The dollar has gained against the mark and most other European currencies over the past year.
